title: Not to divide
hook: what he hears here he does not repeat there to set people apart (DN 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mirror, the Buddha's tool for Rahula: before, during and after. Your line: look in the mirror.

It starts so innocently. Can I tell you something? Don't say I said this. And then a sentence moves from one room to another, from one friend to the next, and arrives a little bigger than it left. By the end of the week, two people who used to get lunch together aren't speaking, and neither is quite sure why. It can happen in an office, a family, a group chat. The sutta that opens the Long Discourses has a line about exactly this.
screen: `DON'T SAY I SAID THIS.` → `ONE ROOM TO THE NEXT.` → `TWO FRIENDS, NOT SPEAKING.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Brahmajala, the all-embracing net, and near its start it lists what an ordinary person might praise in the Buddha. Several of the items are about speech. One is about pisuṇā vācā, divisive speech, the second of the four guards. And the description is precise. What he hears in one place, he doesn't repeat in another to set people there against the people here. What he hears there, he doesn't repeat here. That's the mechanism of gossip, named exactly. Information isn't the problem. Carrying it in order to split people is. The sutta doesn't stop at refusing. It turns the guard into a job. In T. W. Rhys Davids's translation, he lives "as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends". The passage goes on to call him a peacemaker who speaks words that make for peace. So this guard has two halves: don't carry the sentence that splits, and when you can, carry the sentence that mends. No vows, no robes. Just what you do with something you heard by the coffee machine. Over time, people tend to notice who repeats things, and who doesn't. The tradition takes it seriously enough to put it in two places: here on the path, and in the monks' own code, which has a specific offense for tale-bearing between monks.
screen: `PISUṆĀ VĀCĀ: SPEECH THAT SPLITS.` · `HEARD HERE, NOT REPEATED THERE.` · `A BINDER TOGETHER.` · `THE ONE OTHERS TRUST.` · then, large: `NOT TO DIVIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you heard recently about someone, the kind of thing that travels, and notice the small pull to pass it on. Don't fight it; just feel it, and let it sit there. Then picture the two people it would land between, still speaking, still getting lunch, and rest in the quiet of a sentence not carried.
Pisuna vaca, divisive speech. In the first of the Long Discourses, the Buddha doesn't carry words to split people; he binds together those who are divided.
Your line: a sentence that mends. Heard here, and not repeated there. Until next time.

howItsDone: Buddhists treat abstaining from divisive speech as part of right speech; monastics keep a rule against tale-bearing among monks, and some teachers suggest simply letting gossip stop with you.

original.note: Pali pisuṇā vācā: divisive or slanderous speech, the second of the four kinds right speech gives up.

chat.says: Is it wrong to pass along what I heard about someone at work?
options: The trouble is carrying words to split people; the Buddha bound the divided together.
Only if it's false; repeating something true can never divide anyone.
Only if you get caught; what people don't trace back does no harm.
chat.meaning: In the Brahmajala, he doesn't repeat what he hears to set people against each other. Information isn't the problem; carrying it to split people is.

Brahmajala.meaning: the all-embracing net, the first sutta of the Long Discourses

Long Discourses.meaning: the Digha Nikaya, the Pali collection of long suttas

Rhys Davids.meaning: a scholar who translated Pali texts into English

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1 (Brahmajala Sutta), the section on slander
sources.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, part I

notes: Check Rhys Davids's exact wording in Dialogues of the Buddha I (1899), DN 1 §9: 'Thus does he live as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends, a peacemaker, a lover of peace...'. The voice paraphrases the preceding 'what he hears here he repeats not elsewhere...' sentence rather than quoting it.
Pacittiya 3 (bhikkhupesuñña): confirm numbering and that it concerns tale-bearing among monks.
DN 1 frames these as qualities an ordinary person would praise in the Tathāgata (the 'short section on morality').
